subject: feminism
title: Intersectionality: Crenshaw’s legal word for a harm the single-axis rules kept missing
dek: What intersectionality means as a concrete legal and political argument — not a slogan — then Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1989 essay, the DeGraffenreid, Moore, and Payne Title VII cases, and how Black feminist organizing already named interlocking oppression before the term.
era: legal concept coined 1989; cases 1976–1981; Combahee Statement 1977; Mapping the Margins 1991

thumb.alt: Kimberlé Crenshaw seated, looking toward the camera, photographed in Berlin in 2018.

hero.alt: Portrait of Kimberlé Crenshaw in Berlin in July 2018, seated, wearing a patterned scarf.
hero.caption: Kimberlé Williams Crenshaw, photographed in Berlin in July 2018 by Mohamed Badarne. In 1989, while teaching and writing in U.S. law schools, she published “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex,” the essay that put the word intersectionality into legal scholarship. This picture is decades later. The argument below is from the cases and the text.
hero.credit: Mohamed Badarne / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

honesty: This lesson treats intersectionality as a named legal and political tool with a dated origin, not as a vague personality type or online insult. The core argument follows Crenshaw’s 1989 University of Chicago Legal Forum essay and the district-court records she cites, especially DeGraffenreid v. General Motors (E.D. Mo. 1976). The traffic-intersection analogy appears because Crenshaw used it; this lesson states it as her teaching device and then stays with the hiring and layoff facts. Precursors — Combahee River Collective (1977), Frances Beale, Deborah King, and earlier Black women writers — are named so the word does not erase the older analysis. Photographs of 1970s GM shop floors and of the DeGraffenreid plaintiffs are largely still in copyright; the plant exterior and related public-domain or free-licensed images stand in for place and institution, not for the plaintiffs’ faces. Elsewhere is Brazil in the same decades, not a paired “Asia chapter.”

timeline.label: Combahee River Raid
timeline.detail: 2 June 1863: Harriet Tubman guided Union gunboats up the Combahee River in South Carolina. About 750 enslaved people were freed. The 1970s Boston collective took its name from this raid.

timeline.label: Title VII
timeline.detail: 2 July 1964: President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act. Title VII banned employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. Courts later treated those categories as separate axes.

timeline.label: DeGraffenreid
timeline.detail: DeGraffenreid v. General Motors Assembly Division, 413 F. Supp. 142 (E.D. Mo. 1976). Five Black women challenged GM’s seniority layoffs. The court refused a combined race-and-sex claim.

timeline.label: Combahee Statement
timeline.detail: April 1977: the Combahee River Collective published its Statement. It described racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression as interlocking, and rejected ranking one liberation above another.

timeline.label: All the Women Are White…
timeline.detail: Gloria T. Hull, Patricia Bell Scott, and Barbara Smith edited All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, But Some of Us Are Brave (1982). The title named the same erasure Crenshaw later mapped in doctrine.

timeline.label: Demarginalizing
timeline.detail: Kimberlé Crenshaw published “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. The word intersectionality entered legal scholarship.

timeline.label: Mapping the Margins
timeline.detail: Crenshaw published “Mapping the Margins: Intersectionality, Identity Politics, and Violence against Women of Color” in the Stanford Law Review, extending the analysis beyond employment into rape and domestic violence.

timeline.label: Marcha das Mulheres Negras
timeline.detail: 18 November 2015: tens of thousands of Black women marched on Brasília. Brazilian Black feminist organizing had its own vocabulary; the march made the scale visible nationally.

watch.title: Kimberlé Crenshaw — The Urgency of Intersectionality (TEDWomen, 2016)
watch.note: Crenshaw’s own later talk. She walks through the Say Her Name problem: why Black women’s names often drop out of public attention to police violence. Useful after you have read the 1989 argument, not as a substitute for it.

read.title: Kimberlé Crenshaw — “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (University of Chicago Legal Forum, 1989)
read.note: Open PDF via Chicago Unbound. The primary text for this capsule. DeGraffenreid, Moore, and Payne are worked through in detail.

read.title: Kimberlé Crenshaw — “Mapping the Margins” (Stanford Law Review, 1991)
read.note: Second major essay: identity politics, rape, and domestic violence when race and gender are treated as separable. DOI; full text often via university access or open archives.

read.title: Combahee River Collective — “A Black Feminist Statement” (April 1977)
read.note: The Statement that named interlocking oppressions twelve years before Crenshaw’s legal term. Multiple stable reprints circulate; this is one commonly used classroom PDF.

read.title: DeGraffenreid v. General Motors Assembly Div., 413 F. Supp. 142 (E.D. Mo. 1976)
read.note: The district-court opinion Crenshaw uses as Exhibit A. Read the court’s own language about “super-remedy” and combined claims.

read.title: Frances M. Beale — “Double Jeopardy: To Be Black and Female” (1969/1970)
read.note: Earlier Black feminist framing of compounded race and sex oppression. Pre-dates both Combahee and Crenshaw.

read.title: Patricia Hill Collins — Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised later)
read.note: Near-contemporary synthesis. Collins’s “matrix of domination” is a related sociological vocabulary, not a synonym invented by Crenshaw.

fun_fact.title: The collective’s name is a Civil War military operation
fun_fact.text: The Combahee River Collective did not invent a poetic river name. On 2 June 1863 Harriet Tubman guided Union gunboats up the Combahee River in the South Carolina Lowcountry. Soldiers of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteer Infantry, many of them formerly enslaved, took part. Roughly 750 people were freed in that raid. Tubman is the only woman known to have led a U.S. military operation during the Civil War. When Black feminists in Boston chose the name in the 1970s, they were pointing at that history of Black women’s leadership under fire, not at a metaphor.

image.alt: Nineteenth-century illustration of Union soldiers and freed people during the Combahee River Raid.
image.caption: Period illustration of the June 1863 Combahee River Raid. Harriet Tubman guided the operation; hundreds of enslaved people reached Union boats.

glossary.explain: Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1989 name for how race and sex (and later other axes) can combine into a distinct harm that single-axis antidiscrimination rules and single-issue politics fail to see. Not a personality label; a diagnostic of overlapping structures.

American legal scholar, born 1959 in Canton, Ohio. Taught at UCLA School of Law and Columbia Law School. Coined “intersectionality” in her 1989 essay “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex.” Also a central figure in Critical Race Theory.

glossary.term: Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex
glossary.explain: Crenshaw’s 1989 article in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. Analyzes Title VII cases to show how Black women’s claims disappear when race and sex are treated as mutually exclusive categories.

aliases: Mapping the Margins: Intersectionality, Identity Politics, and Violence against Women of Color
glossary.explain: Crenshaw’s 1991 Stanford Law Review article. Applies intersectionality to rape and domestic violence, and critiques identity politics that isolate race from gender.

Crenshaw’s term for antidiscrimination analysis that treats race discrimination and sex discrimination as separate tracks. Under that frame, a plaintiff must fit “race” or “sex,” not the compound experience of being a Black woman.

aliases: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
glossary.explain: The employment-discrimination title of the 1964 Civil Rights Act. Bars discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The cases in this lesson turn on how courts read those listed grounds.
Landmark U.S. federal statute signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on 2 July 1964. Title VII is the employment chapter used in DeGraffenreid and related cases.

aliases: DeGraffenreid v. General Motors Assembly Div.
glossary.explain: 1976 federal district-court case in St. Louis. Five Black women challenged GM’s seniority-based layoffs after a period when the company had hired almost no Black women. The court refused to recognize a combined race-and-sex class.
Lead plaintiff named in DeGraffenreid v. General Motors. One of five Black women who sued over hiring and layoff patterns that, on Crenshaw’s reading, targeted Black women specifically.

U.S. auto manufacturer. The St. Louis Truck Assembly / Natural Bridge plant complex is the workplace setting for DeGraffenreid. Evidence in the case: GM hired no Black women before 1964; Black women hired after 1970 were then cut by seniority.

Title VII case Crenshaw discusses alongside DeGraffenreid. A Black woman plaintiff’s attempt to represent women generally was constrained because courts doubted she could speak for white women’s sex-discrimination claims.

Fifth Circuit Title VII litigation Crenshaw cites. Black women plaintiffs were limited in representing Black employees as a whole; the court feared their sex claims would conflict with Black men’s interests.
Black feminist group active in Boston in the 1970s. Members included Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, and Demita Frazier among others. Published the Combahee River Collective Statement in April 1977.

April 1977 political statement. Declared that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression interlock, and that the Collective’s politics came from their own identity. Major precursor language for what Crenshaw later named intersectionality.
Abolitionist and Underground Railroad conductor, c. 1822–1913. Led the June 1863 Combahee River Raid. The Boston collective named itself after that operation.
2 June 1863 Union raid up the Combahee River in South Carolina, guided by Harriet Tubman. About 750 enslaved people were freed. Source of the Collective’s name.
Black feminist writer and SNCC-era activist. Her essay “Double Jeopardy: To Be Black and Female” (c. 1969–1970) named compounded race and sex oppression before Combahee and Crenshaw.

glossary.term: Double Jeopardy: To Be Black and Female
glossary.explain: Frances Beale’s late-1960s/1970 essay on the simultaneous pressures of racism and sexism on Black women. An early analytical vocabulary for compound harm.

Sociologist whose 1988 article “Multiple Jeopardy, Multiple Consciousness” analyzed the interactive — not merely additive — effects of race, gender, and class. Published the year before Crenshaw’s legal essay.
Deborah King’s term for interactive, compounding oppressions. Distinct wording from Crenshaw’s intersectionality, aimed at a similar analytical problem.
American sociologist. Black Feminist Thought (1990) developed the “matrix of domination” as a way to map intersecting systems of power. Near-contemporary with Crenshaw’s legal work.

Patricia Hill Collins’s concept for how intersecting oppressions are organized across structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, and interpersonal domains. Related to, not identical with, Crenshaw’s legal term.

Black feminist writer and organizer; member of the Combahee River Collective; co-editor of All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, But Some of Us Are Brave (1982); co-founder of Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press.
Black feminist organizer and writer; member of the Combahee River Collective; sister of Barbara Smith.
Black feminist organizer; member of the Combahee River Collective and a signer of the 1977 Statement.

glossary.term: All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, But Some of Us Are Brave
aliases: But Some of Us Are Brave
glossary.explain: 1982 Black women’s studies anthology edited by Gloria T. Hull, Patricia Bell Scott, and Barbara Smith. The title states the erasure intersectionality later diagnoses in law.
Scholar and poet; co-editor of All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, But Some of Us Are Brave (1982).
Scholar; co-editor of All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, But Some of Us Are Brave (1982).

Legal-academic movement beginning in the late 1980s that examines how law produces and maintains racial hierarchy. Crenshaw was among the early organizers of CRT workshops. Intersectionality is one tool inside that wider project.
Student-edited law journal at the University of Chicago Law School. Published Crenshaw’s 1989 Demarginalizing essay.
Law journal that published Crenshaw’s 1991 “Mapping the Margins.”
Law school at the University of California, Los Angeles, where Crenshaw has long taught. One of her two primary academic bases with Columbia.
Law school at Columbia University in New York, where Crenshaw also holds a faculty appointment.
General Motors assembly complex in north St. Louis at Natural Bridge Avenue and Union Boulevard. Operated for decades; closed in the 1980s. Workplace geography behind DeGraffenreid.
Workplace rule that lays off newest workers first. When an employer excluded a group until recently, seniority turns past exclusion into present job loss. Central fact pattern in DeGraffenreid.

Phrase used by the DeGraffenreid court: plaintiffs should not “combine statutory remedies to create a new ‘super-remedy.’” Crenshaw quotes it to show how compound claims were framed as excess rather than accuracy.

Politics organized around a shared social identity. Crenshaw’s Mapping the Margins critiques versions that isolate race from gender (or gender from race) and therefore drop women of color at the join.
Campaign associated with the African American Policy Forum (which Crenshaw co-founded) to make Black women and girls killed by police visible in public memory. Featured in Crenshaw’s 2016 TED talk.
Think tank co-founded by Kimberlé Crenshaw and Luke Charles Harris. Home of Say Her Name and later public education on intersectionality.

Brazilian intellectual, anthropologist, and Black feminist (1935–1994). Developed amefricanidade / amefricanidade to name African diasporic experience in the Americas, including Brazil’s racial-sexual order. Working in the same decades as Crenshaw, in a different legal and colonial history.

Lélia Gonzalez’s concept (also spelled amefricanidade in some texts) for the shared, historically shaped experience of African-descended peoples in the Americas. A Brazilian analytical vocabulary for race, gender, and coloniality — not a translation of Crenshaw’s term.
National march of Black women in Brasília on 18 November 2015. Tens of thousands participated. A later Brazilian public demonstration of Black feminist organizing at scale.
U.S. president who signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 on 2 July 1964, creating Title VII.
Crenshaw’s October 2016 TEDWomen talk. Uses audience silence around Black women’s names to show whose deaths the public already knows how to mourn.

Abolitionist and women’s-rights advocate (c. 1797–1883). Her 1851 Akron speech, later framed as “Ain’t I a Woman?”, is often cited as an early insistence that “woman” must include Black women. Covered in this archive’s First Wave capsule.

Law professor whose October 1991 Senate testimony about Clarence Thomas is a pivot in this archive’s Third Wave capsule. Intersectionality helps explain why a Black woman’s harassment claim was heard through competing single-axis scripts.
Writer and theorist (1952–2021). Ain’t I a Woman (1981) and later work analyzed how mainstream feminism centered white women. Appears in Second and Third Wave capsules in this archive.

sections.title: The word came late; the problem was already in the file

blocks.text: This archive already has four Feminism capsules numbered as waves. First Wave ends around the vote. Second Wave runs through the Equal Rights Amendment’s failed deadline and includes the Combahee River Collective Statement of April 1977. Third Wave opens with Anita Hill in 1991 and gives Kimberlé Crenshaw’s essays a few careful paragraphs. Fourth Wave follows hashtags and street marches in the 2010s. Those lessons mention intersectionality. They do not stop long enough to watch a court refuse a claim, or to read how the refusal was written.

Intersectionality is not a fifth wave. It is a tool for seeing what wave stories and single-issue statutes keep dropping. In U.S. employment law after 1964, race discrimination and sex discrimination were written as separate grounds. A plaintiff who was harmed as a Black woman could find that each separate test was satisfied by someone else’s body: the company hired Black men, so race looked fine; it hired white women, so sex looked fine; the people at the overlap still lost the jobs. Crenshaw’s 1989 essay gave that failure a name and walked through the cases. Black feminist organizers had already described interlocking oppression in print. The legal word arrived afterward.

blocks.alt: President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, surrounded by officials and civil rights leaders.
blocks.caption: President Lyndon B. Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act of 1964 on 2 July 1964. Title VII of that statute banned employment discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The list made separate categories available to plaintiffs. It did not tell courts what to do when the harm sat in more than one category at once.
blocks.credit: Cecil Stoughton, White House Press Office / public domain

blocks.text: Hold two dates next to each other. April 1977: Combahee publishes a Statement that refuses to rank race liberation against sex liberation. 1989: Crenshaw publishes “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. Twelve years apart. Same structural complaint, different genres — a movement document and a law-review argument. This lesson stays with the legal argument long enough to see the mechanism, then looks sideways to Brazil in the same decades, where Lélia Gonzalez was building a different vocabulary for race and gender under a different state.

Intersectionality, in Crenshaw’s usage, is a way to describe how systems of power can combine so that the person standing at the join is not merely “doubly” burdened in an additive sense. The point is structural: institutions, doctrines, and movements often design their remedies around a prototype person who has one disadvantage and otherwise fits the dominant pattern. Remedies built for that prototype can miss the person who never fit it.

In antidiscrimination law, the prototype for “race plaintiff” tended to be a Black man. The prototype for “sex plaintiff” tended to be a white woman. A Black woman’s complaint could fail both prototypes at once. Crenshaw called this a single-axis framework: analysis that treats race and sex as mutually exclusive categories of experience. Under that framework, the most accurate description of the harm — discrimination against Black women as Black women — sounded to the court like an improper request for a special subcategory.

Crenshaw illustrated the idea with a traffic intersection. Discrimination, she wrote, can travel along a race road and a sex road; a collision at the join is not always assignable to one road alone. That picture is hers, from 1989, and it is a teaching device. The evidence that matters is not the metaphor. It is the hiring log, the layoff list, and the judicial sentence that forbids combining the statutes.

What the concept is not: a scorecard of identities, a rule that the most marginalized person always wins an argument, or a synonym for “diversity.” Used carefully, it asks a narrower question. Which harms become invisible when our categories and our organizations are built as if people have only one politically relevant axis at a time?

blocks.alt: Kimberlé Crenshaw speaking into a microphone at a public event.
blocks.caption: Crenshaw speaking at a Heinrich Böll Foundation event. By the 2010s the word intersectionality had left the law review and entered journalism, activism, and backlash. The 1989 essay is still the cleanest place to see what she was trying to fix in doctrine.

sections.title: DeGraffenreid, Moore, Payne — and the sentence about a “super-remedy”

blocks.text: In DeGraffenreid v. General Motors Assembly Division, decided in 1976 by the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, five Black women sued General Motors. Their workplace was the company’s St. Louis assembly operation. The complaint was about hiring history and about layoffs under a seniority system. Evidence summarized in the litigation and later by Crenshaw showed a stark pattern: General Motors had not hired Black women before 1964. After 1970, Black women were hired into the plant. When recession layoffs came, the seniority rule — last hired, first fired — pushed those same Black women out.

blocks.alt: Exterior of the former General Motors Chevrolet plant on Union Boulevard in St. Louis.
blocks.caption: Former General Motors facility at 3809 Union Boulevard, St. Louis — part of the sprawling Natural Bridge / Union Boulevard assembly complex that employed thousands for decades and closed in the 1980s. DeGraffenreid was litigated against GM’s St. Louis assembly division. This is the plant as architecture and address, not a photograph of the plaintiffs.
blocks.credit: Joseph Hampel / Missouri Historical Society / public domain

blocks.text: The plaintiffs tried to sue as Black women — as people harmed by the combination of race and sex discrimination. The district court refused that framing. Judge’s language, quoted by Crenshaw and still readable in the opinion: plaintiffs had cited no decision treating Black women as a special class; they should not “combine statutory remedies to create a new ‘super-remedy’” beyond what the drafters intended. The lawsuit, the court said, must be examined as race discrimination, or sex discrimination, or either — “but not a combination of both.”

Once the claim was split, each half could be made to fail. On sex: General Motors had hired women for years before 1964 — white women. So a pure sex-discrimination story about historical exclusion looked weak, because “women” as a category appeared in the workforce. On race and seniority: courts often upheld last-hired-first-fired systems unless plaintiffs could show the system perpetuated illegal discrimination in a way the doctrine already recognized. Black men had been in the plant. The people missing from the older workforce, and then missing again after the layoff, were Black women. The single-axis tests had somewhere else to look.

Crenshaw pairs DeGraffenreid with two other Title VII matters. In Moore v. Hughes Helicopter, a Black woman’s effort to represent a broader class of women ran into judicial skepticism that she could represent white women’s sex-discrimination claims. In Payne v. Travenol, Black women plaintiffs faced limits on representing Black employees generally, because courts worried their sex claims might diverge from Black men’s interests. Read together, the pattern is ugly and clear. Black women were too different from white women to stand in for “women,” and too different from Black men to stand in for “Blacks,” yet not different enough to be recognized as their own protected class when they asked for that recognition directly.

“Demarginalizing” is the essay that walks through these cases and then turns the same lens on feminist theory and antiracist politics. Crenshaw’s charge is not only that courts failed. It is that movements can reproduce the same single-axis design: a feminism that centers white women’s experience as “women’s,” and an antiracism that centers Black men’s experience as “Black,” each leaving Black women to argue for admission into someone else’s prototype.

blocks.alt: Interior view of the Arthur W. Diamond Library at Columbia Law School.
blocks.caption: Arthur W. Diamond Library, Columbia Law School. Crenshaw holds faculty appointments at Columbia Law and UCLA School of Law. The 1989 essay was written inside this profession — clinics, journals, doctrine — not as a later social-media slogan.
blocks.credit: Ajay Suresh / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0

sections.title: Combahee, Beale, King, Collins — the analysis without Crenshaw’s noun

blocks.text: If you only learn the 1989 coinage, you will misdate the insight. In April 1977 the Combahee River Collective — Black feminists in Boston, among them Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, and Demita Frazier — published “A Black Feminist Statement.” They wrote that they were committed to struggling against racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression, and that the synthesis of those oppressions created the conditions of their lives. They refused to choose which liberation line to stand in. That is interlocking oppression stated in movement prose.

They named themselves after Harriet Tubman’s June 1863 Combahee River Raid, when Union boats moved upriver in South Carolina and hundreds of enslaved people reached freedom. The name was a historical claim about Black women’s leadership, not a decorative place-name.

Still earlier, Frances Beale’s “Double Jeopardy: To Be Black and Female” (around 1969–1970) described compounded race and sex pressures on Black women inside and outside movement organizations. In 1988, the year before Demarginalizing, sociologist Deborah King published “Multiple Jeopardy, Multiple Consciousness,” arguing that race, gender, and class interact rather than simply stack. In 1990 Patricia Hill Collins published Black Feminist Thought and developed the “matrix of domination” as a map of how intersecting oppressions are organized across domains of power. Different disciplines, overlapping problem.

In 1982 Gloria T. Hull, Patricia Bell Scott, and Barbara Smith edited the anthology All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, But Some of Us Are Brave. The title is a diagnosis you can hang next to DeGraffenreid. When “women” defaults to white and “Blacks” defaults to men, the remainder is not a rounding error. It is a structural absence.

blocks.alt: South entrance of the UCLA School of Law.
blocks.caption: South entrance, UCLA School of Law. Crenshaw has taught generations of students here while also based at Columbia. Intersectionality moved from a law-forum essay into classrooms, clinics, and, eventually, wider public speech.

sections.title: Brazil was not waiting for a Chicago law-forum noun

blocks.text: While U.S. courts were splitting Title VII claims and Crenshaw was writing Demarginalizing, Brazilian intellectual Lélia Gonzalez (1935–1994) was elaborating amefricanidade — a concept for African diasporic life in the Americas that insisted on race, gender, and the afterlife of slavery and colonialism together. Gonzalez worked as an anthropologist, activist, and public thinker under and after Brazil’s military dictatorship. Her vocabulary is not a translation of intersectionality. It answers a Brazilian racial order, a Portuguese-language public sphere, and a different legal history. Put her next to Crenshaw as a contemporary, not as a derivative.

blocks.alt: Portrait photograph of Brazilian intellectual Lélia Gonzalez.
blocks.caption: Lélia Gonzalez, photographed by Cezar Loureiro. Gonzalez’s amefricanidade work in the 1970s–1980s analyzed race and sex in Brazil without waiting for a U.S. law-review term to arrive.

blocks.text: On 18 November 2015, decades after Gonzalez’s main essays, tens of thousands of Black women marched on Brasília in the Marcha das Mulheres Negras. The march’s scale belongs to a Brazilian Black feminist continuum — organizations, writers, and electoral politics that had been building for years. It is a useful later image of public force. It is not proof that Brazil “received” intersectionality from the United States. The analytical work was already local.

blocks.alt: Crowds of Black women marching in Brasília during the 2015 Marcha das Mulheres Negras.
blocks.caption: Marcha das Mulheres Negras, Brasília, 18 November 2015. A national demonstration by Black women in Brazil. Contemporaneous elsewhere in this lesson means Gonzalez’s generation beside Crenshaw’s; the march shows later continuity and size.
blocks.credit: Ministério da Cultura / Flickr / CC BY 2.0

sections.title: The word escapes the law review

blocks.text: In 1991 Crenshaw published “Mapping the Margins” in the Stanford Law Review. The essay takes intersectionality into rape law, domestic-violence shelters, and identity politics. Shelters and police practices designed around a default white woman’s path through the system could fail women of color at every step — language access, immigration fear, community policing relationships, stereotypes about who is a “real” victim. Again the mechanism is institutional design around a prototype.

Through the 1990s and 2000s the word moved into sociology, public health, education, and activist speech. Crenshaw co-founded the African American Policy Forum. The Say Her Name campaign pressed a simple archival point: public mourning for police violence often knew how to say men’s names and went quiet on women’s. Her 2016 TEDWomen talk, “The Urgency of Intersectionality,” turns that silence into a live demonstration with an audience.

Widening use brought caricature. By the late 2010s “intersectionality” could mean, in a newspaper column or a comment thread, almost anything about identity. That drift is real. It does not erase the 1976 court opinion, the 1977 Statement, or the 1989 essay. When the word gets mushy, the cure is to go back to the layoff list and the sentence about a super-remedy.

Inside this Capsules archive, the practical payoff is reading discipline. When a Feminism lesson says “women,” ask which women the evidence actually shows. When a race lesson says “Black,” ask whether Black women are in the frame or only in a footnote. Intersectionality is one trained habit for noticing the join before the story moves on.

When a rule, a movement, or a syllabus is built around a single axis, who has to disappear for the categories to stay neat — and what would the filing, the march, or the reading list look like if that person were treated as the central case instead of the exception?
